consensus_summary: Shadow is a context-dependent biblical image, chiefly denoting either divine protection and refuge or an incomplete typological representation of realities fulfilled in Christ; transience and death/darkness are other established senses.
book_summary: Shadow is an object or activity shaped by a substance that marks the extent of its covering. Israel’s appointed times and assemblies are thus Christ’s shadow, while the Shadow of Death is its opposite.
consensus_core_identification: In the relevant New Testament theological sense, a shadow is an anticipatory or incomplete representation of Christ or heavenly reality; in protective texts, it signifies shelter under a covering presence.
book_core_identification: A shadow is a substance-shaped representation that delineates the reach of that substance’s covering, exemplified by sacred times and assemblies as the shadow of Christ.
boundary_disagreement: The book combines the consensus’s typological and protective senses into one structural definition and makes being shaped by a substance and marking its covering boundary constitutive. It especially classifies appointed times and holy assemblies under this definition and treats the Shadow of Death as an opposite, whereas the consensus treats death-shadow as another contextual sense. This may exclude typological cases that do not meet the book’s covering-and-boundary condition and reclassifies protection from a parallel meaning into part of the core mechanism.
material_contradiction: There is no direct contradiction in identifying festivals, the law, and sanctuary institutions as shadows related to Christ or heavenly realities. The material difference lies in the book’s added claim that a shadow marks the reach of the substance’s covering and in its oppositional treatment of the Shadow of Death, neither of which is part of the consensus core.
rationale: The book preserves the recognizable typological referent emphasized in Colossians 2 and Hebrews, while integrating the protective imagery of Psalm 91. It therefore does not replace the consensus identification. However, it materially refines the category by supplying a geometric/covering condition, foregrounding appointed assemblies, and reorganizing death-shadow as an opposite rather than merely another sense. These are substantive boundary and classification changes, supporting REFINED rather than MATCH or DIVERGENT.
strongest_objection: Colossians 2:16–17 and Hebrews 8:5 and 10:1 strongly support festivals, law, and sanctuary service as shadows of Christ or heavenly things, and Psalm 91:1 supports protective covering. But the printed citations do not clearly establish that every shadow is shaped like its substance, that it marks the precise reach and boundary of covering, or that the Shadow of Death is categorically its opposite.
